Medicine-07.question: ১) Psychiatric illness that risks suicide
২) Bell’s palsy
Medicine-07.option1: Lower motor neuron lesion of 7th nerve palsy
Medicine-07.option2: Upper motor neuron lesion of 7th nerve palsy
Medicine-07.exp:
Bell's palsy is an idiopathic lower motor neuron (LMN) paralysis of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). It causes acute unilateral weakness of all muscles of facial expression, including the forehead.

Typical features:

  • Inability to wrinkle the forehead

  • Inability to close the eye

  • Drooping of the angle of the mouth

  • Loss of nasolabial fold

  • Hyperacusis and loss of taste (anterior two-thirds of the tongue) may occur

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Lower motor neuron lesion of 7th nerve palsy — Correct. Bell's palsy is an LMN facial nerve palsy.

  • B. Upper motor neuron lesion of 7th nerve palsy — UMN lesions spare the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation.

  • C. Both of them — Incorrect.

  • D. None of them — Incorrect.

High-yield Recall

LMN Facial Palsy (Bell's palsy) UMN Facial Palsy
Whole ipsilateral face affected Forehead spared
Cannot wrinkle forehead Forehead wrinkling preserved
Cannot close eye Eye closure usually preserved
Mouth deviates to opposite side Mouth weakness only in lower face

Exam pearl: Forehead involvement distinguishes an LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy) from an UMN facial palsy due to stroke.

Medicine-07.question: ৩) Mood stabilizing drugs excludes
৪) Which may help to establish type of epilepsy & guide therapy?
Medicine-07.exp:
EEG is the most important investigation for classifying the type of epilepsy and guiding antiepileptic drug therapy. It detects epileptiform discharges (spikes, sharp waves, spike-and-wave complexes) that help distinguish focal from generalized epilepsy.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. ECG — Used to evaluate cardiac causes of syncope, not to classify epilepsy.

  • B. EEG — Correct. Helps establish the type of epilepsy and guides treatment.

  • C. MRI — Identifies structural brain lesions causing epilepsy but does not classify seizure type as effectively as EEG.

  • D. NCS (Nerve Conduction Study) — Used for peripheral neuropathies, not epilepsy.

High-yield Recall

Investigation Main Use in Epilepsy
EEG Classifies epilepsy and guides therapy
MRI brain Detects structural lesions (tumor, cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis)
CT brain Acute evaluation (trauma, hemorrhage)
ECG Excludes cardiac syncope
NCS Peripheral nerve disorders

Exam pearl: EEG classifies epilepsy; MRI identifies the underlying structural cause.

Medicine-07.question: ৫) Not a negative symptom of schizophrenia
৬) Most common pathogen of meningitis?
Medicine-07.exp:
Overall, viral meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis, especially due to enteroviruses (e.g., Coxsackievirus, Echovirus). It is generally milder and self-limiting compared with bacterial meningitis.

If the question specifically asked for the most common bacterial cause, the answer would depend on age (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae in adults).

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Virus — Correct. Most common overall cause of meningitis.

  • B. Bacteria — Causes the most severe forms but is not the most common overall.

  • C. Fungus — Occurs mainly in immunocompromised patients.

  • D. Parasite — Rare cause of meningitis.

High-yield Recall

Type of Meningitis Common Cause
Viral (most common overall) Enteroviruses
Bacterial (adults) Streptococcus pneumoniae
Bacterial (adolescents/young adults) Neisseria meningitidis
Fungal Cryptococcus neoformans (immunocompromised)

Exam pearl: Overall, viruses are the most common cause of meningitis, whereas bacterial meningitis is the most life-threatening and requires urgent antibiotic therapy.

Medicine-07.question: ৭) Adverse effect of antipsychotic drugs due to dopamine blockade
৮) Most common virus for meningitis?
Medicine-07.exp:
Enteroviruses (especially Coxsackievirus and Echovirus) are the most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis worldwide. They account for the majority of cases, particularly in children and young adults.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. HSV-1 — More commonly causes encephalitis, especially temporal lobe encephalitis.

  • B. HSV-2 — Can cause recurrent viral meningitis (Mollaret meningitis) but is not the most common overall.

  • C. Enterovirus — Correct. Most common viral cause of meningitis.

  • D. VZV — Can cause meningitis, especially in immunocompromised patients, but is less common.

High-yield Recall

Virus Typical CNS Disease
Enterovirus Most common viral meningitis
HSV-1 Encephalitis
HSV-2 Meningitis (especially recurrent)
VZV Meningitis/encephalitis, vasculopathy

Exam pearl: Remember: Enterovirus → meningitis; HSV-1 → encephalitis.

Medicine-07.question: ৯) Mood disorders excludes
১০) Most serious cause of viral encephalitis
Medicine-07.exp:
HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis and the most serious cause of viral encephalitis. It has a predilection for the temporal and frontal lobes, causing:

  • Fever

  • Altered consciousness

  • Seizures

  • Focal neurological deficits

  • Personality and memory changes

Early treatment with intravenous acyclovir markedly reduces mortality and neurological sequelae.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. HSV — Correct. Most serious and most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis.

  • B. VZV — Can cause encephalitis but is less common and generally less frequent than HSV.

  • C. Enterovirus — Common cause of viral meningitis; encephalitis is less common.

  • D. EBV — Rare cause of encephalitis.

High-yield Recall

Virus Typical CNS Disease
HSV-1 Most serious viral encephalitis
Enterovirus Most common viral meningitis
HSV-2 Recurrent viral meningitis
VZV Encephalitis, meningitis, vasculopathy
Rabies virus Fatal encephalitis

Exam pearl: Suspected HSV encephalitis is a medical emergency—start IV acyclovir immediately without waiting for confirmatory test results.

Medicine-07.question: ১১) Which of the following is persistent?
১২) Classical presentation of stroke
Medicine-07.exp:
The classical presentation of stroke is the sudden onset of unilateral (one-sided) weakness or numbness involving the face, arm, and/or leg due to an acute focal neurological deficit.

Other symptoms depend on the area of the brain involved and may include aphasia, visual loss, ataxia, or dysarthria.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Aphasia — Occurs in dominant hemisphere strokes but is not present in all strokes.

  • B. Unilateral weakness — Correct. The most common and classical presentation of stroke.

  • C. Unconsciousness — Usually occurs only in large hemispheric, brainstem, or hemorrhagic strokes.

  • D. Seizure — May occur at stroke onset but is uncommon as the classical presentation.

High-yield Recall

Symptom Association with Stroke
Sudden unilateral weakness Classical presentation
Aphasia Dominant (usually left MCA) stroke
Hemianopia Occipital or posterior circulation stroke
Unconsciousness Large hemorrhage or brainstem stroke
Seizure Uncommon presenting feature

Exam pearl: Remember the FAST mnemonic: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to seek emergency care.
